title: Development of a control task for clarifying the neural mechanisms underlying tool-use behavior in rats (Rattus norvegicus)
author: Nagano

steps.title: Prepare and handle subjects
steps.instruction: Use eight experimentally naïve three‑month‑old male Brown‑Norway rats (IDs BN21–BN28). House each individually in wire cages. Record average weight 253.38 g (SD = 9.28 g). Maintain rats at ~85 % of free‑feeding weight during training, allowing ~10 g weight gain per month. Keep animal room on a 12‑h light/dark cycle (lights on 08:00–20:00).

steps.title: Habituate rats to handling and food
steps.instruction: Handle each rat for 5 min per day for 5 consecutive days. Introduce feeding restriction on day 3 to achieve target body weight. From day 3, habituate rats to the chocolate‑flavored loop cereal reward by placing the cereal in their home cage for 3 days.

steps.title: Set up experimental apparatus
steps.instruction: Place a transparent acrylic experimental box (21.0 cm W × 21.0 cm L × 25.6 cm H) on a desk. Mount a transparent sliding door (21.0 cm W × 32.0 cm H × 0.3 cm thick) on the front; use either a solid door or a door with a square hole (1.5 cm W × 1.5 cm H, centered horizontally, hole height 21.0 cm). Position an experimental board in front of the door: a white cutting mat (23.0 cm W × 32.0 cm L × 0.3 cm thick) placed on a transparent acrylic board (23.9 cm W × 33.5 cm H × 0.5 cm thick). Insert a central transparent acrylic partition (0.5 cm W × 29.0 cm L × 1.0 cm H) in the middle of the board for all sessions except the shaping phase. Lay black drawing paper underneath the box. Ensure a 1.7 cm gap between the lower edge of the sliding door and the board surface when the door is open.

steps.title: Fabricate hooks and fake foods
steps.instruction: Create 73 hook‑shaped objects: 19 Hooks A and 18 Hooks B from aluminum, 36 Hooks C from iron wire; all coated with dental resin (Ostron II Blue) and light‑blue. Each hook ≤ 2.3 cm W × 6.0 cm L × 1.0 cm H. Weigh Hooks A + B together with attached fake food so that each pair matches the weight of a Hook C (2.90–3.10 g). Prepare 73 fake foods: small rounded aluminum foil pieces covered with a mixture of 31.09 g powder, liquid resin, and 5.52 g cocoa powder; size ≤ 0.8–1.5 cm W × 0.7–1.0 cm H, resembling a chocolate‑flavored loop cereal. Glue fake food to the interior of Hook A (in contact with the bend) and to Hook B leaving a 1.0 cm gap; Hook C receives no fake food. Keep 36 additional fake foods unattached for use as incorrect options (secured to the board with double‑sided tape).

steps.title: Hook‑pulling shaping and training
steps.instruction: Conduct hook‑pulling training consisting of 40 trials per session. Keep the sliding door with the square hole open throughout, maintaining the 1.7 cm gap. At session start, place the rat in the box and position Hook A at the centre according to the current phase. Progress through six phases, increasing the distance between the fake food and the door by 1.0 cm after the rat meets the criterion of the previous phase. Phase 1 distance = 0 cm; Phase 6 is the final distance. In Phase 1, shape behavior by rewarding any touch (paw, nose, mouth) with food, then any pull, and finally only rewarding pulls that bring the fake food into the box. Advance to the next phase after five successful trials; the same five‑success criterion applies to all phases. Use two hook arrangements each day, each presented in half of the trials in a pseudo‑random order. End each trial when the rat pulls the hook so the fake food enters the box (success) – immediately offer a real chocolate reward through the square hole and retrieve the hook – or after 60 s without success, then retrieve the hook.

steps.title: Hook‑choice training sessions
steps.instruction: Run hook‑choice training with 36 trials per session (12 distinct hook‑food arrangements, each presented three times). Use 18 Hooks A and 18 Hooks B (correct options, each with fake food) and 36 Hooks C plus 36 independent fake foods (incorrect options). At the start of each session, place the rat in the box with the sliding door closed; the door‑to‑board gap is 1.7 cm. After positioning the hooks and fake foods, open the door after 3 s to signal trial start. Consider a hook selected when the rat pulls it ≥ 2.0 cm. If the correct hook is selected, immediately retrieve the incorrect hook and its fake food, offer a real food reward through the square hole, then retrieve the correct hook before closing the door. If the incorrect hook is selected, retrieve the correct hook immediately, wait 30 s, close the door without offering a reward, then retrieve the incorrect hook and fake food before closing. If no selection occurs within 60 s, retrieve both options and close the door. Record trials as successful (correct hook pulled and its fake food entered the box within 60 s), failed (incorrect hook or correct hook not pulling fake food into the box), or no‑choice. Continue training until the rat achieves ≥ 30 successful trials in two consecutive sessions. Note: rat BN22 failed to meet this criterion after 83 sessions; its rake‑choice test was performed the next day.

steps.title: Record behavior with video
steps.instruction: Mount a Panasonic HDC‑TM30 video camera above the experimental box and record the rat’s behavior continuously during all training and testing sessions.

steps.title: Rake‑choice test sessions
steps.instruction: Prepare four rake tools (Rakes A–D). Rake A: acrylic blade with resin coating; Rake B: white L‑shaped metal blade with resin; both have a vertical wire glued to the blade end, making them non‑functional when inverted. Rake C appears non‑functional but contains a transparent acrylic plate between two wires under the blade, rendering it functional. Rake D appears functional but has 39 light‑blue embroidery threads glued to the blade bottom, making it non‑functional. All rakes have a vertical wire at the blade end and a wire‑resin handle at the centre. Conduct three test sessions (Test 1, Test 2, Test 3), each in a single day. Tests 1 and 2 present tools whose appearance matches functionality; Test 3 presents a contradiction between appearance and functionality. Between each test, retrain the rat with two sessions of hook‑choice training. During the tests, allow the rat to obtain the real food reward directly by pulling the functional rake; deliver the reward by hand through the square hole as in previous trainings.
